<reason>CON built and sustained a single sharp distinction — disclosure of a seller's own price is well-precedented (baggage fees, APR), while compelled advertising of a rival's price at checkout is not — and forced PRO to concede exactly that point in Rebuttal 2 ("I won't pretend one exists in that exact form"). CON then exploited PRO's pivot from "independent" pickup/direct-order to "the app's own pickup toggle" as an implicit abandonment of the motion as written, and this reframing was never squarely resolved by PRO's closing, which doubled down on the toggle-anchor version rather than defending the literal "independent" language. PRO's underlying asymmetry story (hidden fees, comparison ignorance) was intuitively strong and never disproven as a real problem, but PRO never adequately explained why CON's all-in-pricing alternative wouldn't already resolve most of the harm, nor rebuilt a workable, precedent-backed version of the actual motion after conceding both the precedent gap and the verifiability gap. CON's pressure questions extracted the decisive concessions, and CON's closing crystallized them cleanly; PRO's closing mostly restated the problem rather than repairing the collapsed anchor.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A4 (CON Rebuttal 2), where CON shows that PRO's answer to the verifiability pressure question quietly swapped the motion's "independent" anchor for the app's own pickup price — turning PRO's own concession into proof that the literal motion is either redundant (if the anchor is on-platform) or unworkable (if it truly means independent/direct-order).</best_rebuttal>
